single_run.intro_content: Here you discover Petri nets for one event log with the miners you choose and look at their complexity measures. The page has three sections: the log, the miners and measures, and the run. Esc or Skip ends the tour at any time.
single_run.logsource_content: Two sources: “Upload file” for your own XES or JSON file (recent uploads and the logs of your datasets are listed below), or “Use example” for the bundled example log. The overview shows what is in the log.
single_run.params_content: Choose the miners to run and the measures to compute. The preset bar above saves a selection for later.
single_run.run_content: Start with the button or Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac). The result appears below with the measures, the discovered nets and downloads. The run is listed in the History.

onboarding.step0_p1: Find out which complexity measures of process models and event logs capture the same thing. Load or compute a table of measures, check whether it suits a factor analysis, and read off groups of related measures.
onboarding.step0_p2: This quick tour shows the four things you'll use most.
onboarding.step1_p1: Model complexity analyses measures of Petri nets discovered from event logs, computed with ComFy. Log complexity analyses measures of the event logs themselves, computed with feeed.
onboarding.step1_p2: Both tabs work the same way.
onboarding.step2_p1: Data, Dataset, Suitability, Factors, Loadings: the list of steps shows what each one found and opens it. Back and Next move through them. Changing a setting re-runs the analysis right away. You can download the analysis as CSV, LaTeX or ZIP. An optional sixth step lets Claude propose names for the factors.
onboarding.step2_p2: Hover a control or an (i) to see what it does. The Tour button walks you through the steps.
onboarding.step3_compare: Compare: the factor structures of several analyses side by side, like Tab. 17 of Important Factors.
onboarding.step3_history: History: every dataset and run of your session.
onboarding.step3_inspect: Single log: discover models for one log with miners and measure their complexity.

factor.intro: Five steps lead from the raw measures to the factors, plus an optional interpretation. One step is shown at a time. Switch with the list of steps on the left (on a phone, the row at the top) or with Back and Next. Hover a control or an (i) to see what it does. Esc or Skip ends the tour at any time.
factor.data: Where the data come from: Get started and the bundled datasets, a CSV of your own, or measures computed from your files. Large computations run in the background.
factor.dataset: Check the size of the matrix and what the cleaning removed. You can download the cleaned data as CSV.
factor.suitability: Bartlett and KMO tell you whether a factor analysis makes sense at all. Exclude measures with low MSA here, by hand or with the filter.
factor.factors: The scree plot suggests how many factors to keep. Change the number or the rotation; everything below updates right away.
factor.loadings: The heatmap shows which measures load on which factor; bold values reach the threshold. Export the table as CSV or LaTeX for your paper.
factor.interpretation: Optional: Claude proposes a name and a short reading for each factor. Only the measure names, their definitions and aggregated results are sent, and every request costs money, so it runs only when you press the button. Always check it against the loadings. With a key you can then ask follow-up questions about the analysis.

stability.help: Draws {n} bootstrap samples of the rows, with replacement and a fixed seed, and fits each one with the same measures, factor count and rotation. Tucker's congruence φ and the Hungarian algorithm match the factors of each sample to the factors of this solution; a factor is mirrored where φ is negative. The same assignment rule then applies. The value of a measure is the share of samples in which it keeps its factors.
stability.heywood: In {n} samples a measure reached the Heywood bound although it is not at the bound in this solution. These samples are kept.
stability.none_valid: None of the {samples} samples could be fitted.
stability.stale: The stability shown before belongs to other settings.
stability.failed: The stability could not be computed.
stability.value_tip: Same factors in {pct} of the samples
stability.phi_tip: Mean congruence with the matching factor of the samples; 5th percentile {p5}.
stability.pairs_label: Pairs of measures over the samples
stability.pairs_legend_short: Share of the samples in which two measures share a factor
stability.pairs_legend: Each cell is the share of the valid samples in which the two measures share at least one factor; the darker, the more often. A ring marks the pairs that share a factor in the solution itself.
stability.pairs_cell_more: Share a factor in {pct} of the samples
stability.pairs_cell_together: Share a factor in {pct} of the samples, and in the solution itself

short_set.badge_tip: Represents this dimension in the short set: purity {purity}
short_set.heading: Short set ({n} measure)
short_set.help: One measure per dimension: the assigned measure with the highest purity. Purity is its absolute loading on the dimension minus its largest absolute loading on any other. This gives a few measures to report that do not repeat each other, as the Important Factors paper motivates. Ties go to the higher loading. Read a representative with low stability with care.

help.cleaning: Before the analysis, rows where most values are missing are dropped. Then columns that are not numeric, that have no variance, that have missing values, or that are perfect copies of an earlier column are removed, as in ComFy for log measures. Such columns would distort or break the correlation matrix.
help.bartlett: Bartlett's test checks the null hypothesis that the correlation matrix is an identity matrix, i.e. that the measures are uncorrelated. If p < α, there are correlations that common factors can explain. With many observations the test almost always passes, so read it together with KMO.
help.kmo: The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin criterion compares the correlations between the measures with their partial correlations. Values near 1 mean the measures share common variance. Values near 0 mean the correlations are mostly pairwise. Kaiser's scale (Kaiser 1974): from 0.9 marvelous, 0.8 meritorious, 0.7 middling, 0.6 mediocre, 0.5 miserable, below that unacceptable.
help.msa: The measure of sampling adequacy (MSA) is the KMO value of a single measure. A measure with low MSA shares little with the others and fits no common factor well. Removing it usually raises the overall KMO. Tick a measure to exclude it by hand.
help.msa_filter: As in ComFy, all measures below the threshold are removed and the MSA values are recomputed, until every remaining measure reaches the threshold. If the overall MSA then lies below the threshold, ComFy ends its run. The tool only warns.
help.msa_threshold: The filter removes measures whose MSA is below this value, and the overall KMO counts as adequate from this value on. ComFy and ComFy for log measures use 0.6.
help.bartlett_alpha: The significance level of Bartlett's test: the test passes when p is below α. ComFy and ComFy for log measures use 0.05.
help.scree: The scree plot shows the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix in descending order. Look for the elbow where the curve flattens; factors after it add little. The elbow, the eigenvalue-above-1 rule and the parallel analysis can disagree, so treat them as starting points. The thin line on the right axis shows the cumulative share of the variance that the first principal components explain. The factors of the analysis explain somewhat less, as step 5 shows.
help.eigenvalue: An eigenvalue belongs to a principal component of the correlation matrix. It is the variance the component explains, in units of one standardized measure. The suggestion keeps as many factors as there are eigenvalues above 1 (Kaiser criterion), i.e. as many as there are components that explain more than a single measure.
help.rotation: Rotation turns the factor solution so that each measure loads strongly on as few factors as possible, which makes the factors easier to name. It does not change how much variance the factors explain together. Varimax and quartimax keep the factors uncorrelated; promax and oblimin let them correlate.
help.threshold: Loadings with an absolute value at or above this threshold count as substantial. Which factors a measure joins depends on the assignment rule above. With the largest loading, a measure joins the factor on which its absolute loading is highest, if that loading reaches the threshold. Common values lie between 0.3 and 0.5. ComFy uses 0.35, ComFy for log measures 0.5. Whether a loading exactly on the threshold counts depends on the rule. With the largest loading it counts (≥), and ComFy's report, which only greys loadings below its threshold, leaves it black too. The rules of Important Factors (multiple membership, without cross-loadings) require more than the threshold (>), as the tables of the paper do.
help.loading: A loading says how strongly a measure goes along with a factor. For orthogonal rotations it is the correlation between measure and factor. For oblique rotations the pattern matrix holds regression weights and the structure matrix the correlations. The sign gives the direction: measures with opposite signs on the same factor move in opposite directions. The sign of a whole factor is arbitrary: flipping every sign of a factor changes nothing. The matrix therefore shades by |loading| only.
help.communality: The communality h² is the share of a measure's variance that all kept factors explain together. A low value (below about 0.4) means the factors do not capture the measure well.
help.variance: SS loadings is the sum of squared loadings of a factor. Divided by the number of measures it gives the proportion of the total variance the factor explains; the cumulative row adds these up.
help.groups: Each factor with the measures assigned to it, strongest loading first. Measures in one group capture a similar aspect of complexity; the name of the factor is up to your interpretation. Under multiple membership a measure can be in several groups; a chip names its other factors.
help.communality_threshold: Measures whose communality is below this value are left unassigned, because the factors explain too little of them. ComFy for log measures uses 0.5. The value 0 keeps every measure, except under multiple membership (at least 0.3) and without cross-loadings (at least 0.5).
help.factor_correlations: With an oblique rotation the factors may correlate. Values near 0 mean the factors are nearly independent; large values mean they measure related aspects.
help.assignment: How the loadings turn into factor groups. The largest loading is the default of this tool: each measure joins the factor it loads on most. ComFy's report assigns nothing. It only greys loadings with |λ| below its threshold. Important Factors states two further rules. For Tab. 6–16, a measure also joins every factor whose loading is at most {gap} below its largest (multiple membership), with h² ≥ {h2_multi}. For Tab. 17 (without cross-loadings, justified in the paper with Hair et al.), h² ≥ {h2_hair} applies and cross-loaded measures are left out. The tool applies the rules as the paper states them. Where a table of the paper differs, a note below the rules says so for the bundled datasets. The factor solution is the same under every rule; only the groups change.
help.criteria: Kaiser keeps every factor with an eigenvalue above 1. Parallel analysis (Horn) keeps the factors whose eigenvalue is above the {percentile}th percentile of the eigenvalues of {simulations} random normal datasets of the same size. It is computed on principal components with the fixed seed {seed}. With many observations it comes close to Kaiser. A paper may also fix the number before the analysis. Choosing a criterion sets the number of factors.

interpretation.intro: Claude reads the loadings together with the definitions of the measures and proposes a name and a short interpretation for each factor. Sent to Anthropic are the measure (column) names, their catalog definitions and aggregated results such as loadings and test statistics. Measure values, row labels and file names are not sent. Each request costs money, so it runs only when you ask for it.

rules.alpha_multi: With the paper settings this rule also puts Connector Heterogeneity (CH) in factor 2. Tab. 6 of the paper lists it in dimension 4 only.
rules.inductive_multi: With the paper settings this rule also puts Average connector degree (acd) in factor 2. Tab. 12 of the paper lists it in dimensions 1 and 3 only.
rules.alpha_hair: With the paper settings this rule leaves out Connector Mismatch (MM, h² below {h2_hair}) and the cross-loaded Connector Heterogeneity (CH), so factor 4 stays empty. The Alpha row of Tab. 17 of the paper keeps both.

datasets.hybrid_ilp: Not deterministic. The data differ from Tab. 14–16.
datasets.heuristics: Tab. 13 of the paper prints only the MSA values: 4 measures are left after the filter. The report in the ComFy repository fits 4 factors to them, the tool at most 3.

steps.title: The six steps
steps.p1: Model complexity analyses the ComFy measures of Petri nets, Log complexity the feeed measures of event logs. Both go through the same steps: Data, Dataset, Suitability, Factors, Loadings and an optional Interpretation. Only one step is shown at a time. The list of steps shows what each step found.
steps.p2: The settings row above the steps sums up every choice, marks those that differ from the tool standard and leads to each control. Every change of a setting runs the analysis again.
steps.p3: The tabs at the top are the same on every page: the analyses (Model complexity, Log complexity and Single log) and, set apart on the right, the tools Compare and History. The guide and the settings are in the header and lead back to the tab you came from.

bundled.title: Analyse a published dataset

items.open: Open Model complexity or Log complexity.
items.choose: In Data, choose a dataset of a paper, for example Important Factors: Inductive miner.
items.settings: Choose Paper settings to analyse it as the paper did, or Tool standard for the defaults of ComFy, then Load dataset. The data step stays on screen and shows what was loaded and how to continue.

bundled.p1: With the paper settings, a chip in the settings row says whether the numbers equal the published ComFy report and how the paper's tables relate to it. Get started, the first cards of the bundled datasets in the data step, loads such an analysis in one click. View result then opens its loadings.

own.title: Analyse your own data

items.logs: Event logs (.xes, .xes.gz): for model measures, every log is mined with every miner you choose and every net is measured. For log measures, feeed computes the feature groups you choose. Unfold a group to choose single measures from it, which helps when you have only a few logs and want to keep the number of measures small. Below the choice, the data step shows how many observations and measures that gives, and says when there are too few for a factor analysis.
items.nets: Petri nets (.pnml): every net is measured.
items.csv: A CSV file: one row per observation, one column per measure; a first column of names becomes the row labels.

own.p2: Logs and nets are computed in a run. The tab History shows what is running (“1 running · 37%”) and has a red dot for a failed run you have not seen yet. When a dataset is finished, a notice “… is ready · Open” appears wherever you are. My datasets, a source of the data step, reopens a dataset of the session with the settings of its last analysis.
own.p3: A dataset of nets from several miners has one row per log and miner. The dataset step offers all miners together or one miner at a time, as Important Factors does. Together, the differences between the miners mix into the dimensions and each log counts once per miner. A single miner gives fewer observations. A miner with no more observations than measures cannot be analysed, and below five observations per measure the analysis warns. Compare the miners there opens their factor structures side by side.
own.p4: In the dataset step, each row of a dataset computed from logs has a View this log link. It opens the page Inspect a single log with that log, and for a row of nets with only the miner of that row chosen. This works as long as the log is among the ten newest uploads of the session. Otherwise the page says so.
own.p5: History lists everything from the session, newest first: every dataset of both tabs with the settings of its last analysis, and every run of a single log. A row opens where it belongs, can be aborted while it runs, and can be deleted. Deleting a dataset also deletes the run that computed it, and the other way round.

items.dataset: Dataset: what cleaning left out and why, the descriptive statistics of every measure as ComFy's report prints them, and for a dataset computed from logs or nets the run times and input sizes. Both tables start folded.
items.suitability: Suitability: Bartlett's test, the overall KMO and the MSA of every measure. The MSA filter removes measures in rounds, as ComFy does. You can also exclude measures by hand: one at a time, all together, or those a search finds. If there are too few observations for the analysis, its message says what an observation is and leads to the measures or back to the data.
items.factors: Factors: the scree plot with the Kaiser line and parallel analysis, the count each criterion suggests, and the rotation.
items.loadings: Loadings: above the result, one row holds the rule that assigns measures to factors and the two thresholds; each rule is explained in its tooltip. Below is a matrix (shaded by |loading|, faded where a loading does not count) or a card per dimension. Cross-loadings are ringed.
items.stability: Stability: Check stability under the loadings draws bootstrap samples of the rows (100, 200 or 500), refits each with the same measures, factor count and rotation, and shows for every measure the share of samples in which it keeps its factors. The seed is fixed, so a run can be repeated.
items.short_set: Short set: one measure per dimension, the one assigned to it with the highest purity, for reporting a few measures that do not repeat each other. Copy the short set puts them on the clipboard; a representative with a low stability should be read with care.
items.interpretation: Interpretation: optional, names for the factors, suggested by a language model only on request. It decides nothing. It needs an API key on the server. Model and effort are chosen next to the button: Opus 5.5 gives the best quality, Sonnet 5.5 costs about half and is faster; higher efforts think longer, cost more and take longer. Choices already stored are marked and cost nothing. Precomputed answers come with the bundled datasets, for the default settings and the paper settings. Without a key only what is stored is offered, and without a stored answer for the settings the list of steps says that it is not available here. Under a shown interpretation you can ask follow-up questions about the analysis: Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line, and the answers can contain errors, so check them against the tables. Every question is one request and counts towards the same limits.
items.names: Names: press the title of a factor, on its card or at the head of its column, to name it. Enter keeps the name, Esc cancels. The names appear in the loadings, the factor correlations, the list of steps and every download. They belong to the factor count, the rotation and the rule: changing one of them clears the names, and the toast brings them back. With an interpretation, Use the suggested names takes over its names.
items.correlations: Correlation map: in Suitability, folded until opened. It has one cell per pair of measures: slate for a negative correlation, blue for a positive one, and an outline where |r| ≥ 0.95. The order is by factor or clustered. Point at a cell or use the arrow keys to read the pair and its r. A table under the map has every value. The image icon downloads it like the other figures.
items.sheet: Fact sheet: press the name of a measure, or Enter on it, wherever it appears to open a panel beside the page. The panel shows what the measure is (the description of the tool and the function of ComFy or feeed behind it, with a link to its source), a histogram of its values, its MSA and the filter round that removed it, its communality and uniqueness, its loadings, the five measures it correlates with most, and a button to exclude or include it. The left and right arrow keys page through the list you came from. Esc closes the panel and the focus goes back to the name.

export.title: Take the results into a paper
export.p1: The download menu in the page header has:

items.zip: Analysis (ZIP): the result, the matrix, the tables, report.tex, the figures, correlations.csv, the descriptive statistics, the run times, and a manifest with settings, versions and provenance.
items.report: LaTeX report: report.tex built like the report of ComFy, with the dimensions and the settings. Compile it with latexmk -pdf, or run pdflatex twice, because the widths of long tables only settle in the second run.
items.print: Print view: the whole analysis on A4 pages, to print or save as PDF.
items.tables: The loadings as CSV or LaTeX, and the cleaned dataset as CSV.

export.p2: The image icon at the scree plot, the loadings and the correlation map downloads the figure as SVG (text stays text) or as PNG at 300 dpi. Figures are always light, as wide as the text of a CEUR paper, and labelled in the language of the app.
export.p3: The tag icon in the toolbar names the measures by the short codes of the papers, such as CNC or C_mag. The full name stays in the tooltip. Figures, report and ZIP follow the choice.
export.p4: The link icon copies a link to the analysis of a published dataset with its settings.

compare.title: Compare miners
compare.p1: Compare miners puts the factor structures of several published datasets side by side, like Tab. 17 of Important Factors: which measures form which dimension for which miner. It is the tool Compare, at the right of the tabs, and two cards of Get started open it too. The datasets and the rule are on the left, the result on the right. Notes on a column show as a count in its header and as one folded list below the table.

items.columns: Datasets: choose 2 to 8 of the miners of Important Factors; each is analysed with the settings of its paper. The first four are those of Tab. 17. A link can also request a dataset with its own factor count, such as 4 against 6 factors (Get started).
items.rule: Assignment rule: one rule for every dataset, “Without cross-loadings” as in Tab. 17 to begin with.
items.matrix: By measure: one row per measure, grouped by dimension. Above them, each dataset shows n, the measures after the MSA filter, the KMO, the factors, the rotation and the variance explained. A tinted cell is in the dimension of its row; a ring marks a cross-loading, a dashed outline a measure the MSA filter removed.
items.dimensions: By dimension: a row per dataset with the measures of each dimension, laid out like Tab. 17.
items.pairs: Pairs: a square of the measures. Each cell says in how many of the datasets that analysed both measures the two share a dimension. The numbering of the dimensions does not matter.
items.export: The download menu has the matrix as CSV, the dimensions as a LaTeX table like Tab. 17, and both in a ZIP with a manifest.
items.own: Your own data: Compare the miners in the dataset step makes one column per miner, and Compare in My datasets one column per dataset. The pin icon in the loadings pins the current solution (dataset, miner, factor count, rotation, rule) as a column, so you can put, say, the same dataset with 4 and with 6 factors side by side. Such a column starts from the settings saved with its dataset and lasts for this session.

compare.p2: Each analysis numbers its factors itself, so they are matched first. The first dataset keeps its numbers. The factors of every further dataset go to the dimension with which they share the most measures; where two are equally good, the more alike loadings decide. Tab. 17 renumbered its dimensions by hand, so a number can differ from the paper's. A match that rests on one shared measure is a guess: the tooltip of a cell in the dimension view names the measures it rests on. How the measures are grouped within a dataset does not depend on the numbers.

help.variance: The share of the variance of the measures that the factors explain together.
